stories.headline: Every eliminated MLS team: What worked and what didn't in 2026, what needs improving in 2027?
stories.summary: After every team in MLS is eliminated from postseason contention, ESPN details the best and worst of their seasons, and their priorities for 2027.
stories.body:
The 2026 MLS regular season came to an end Saturday, when all 30 teams were in action for Decision Day. Eighteen clubs continue on in the MLS Cup playoffs, but for the other 12, the long offseason begins now.

Preseasons for these sides won't begin until well into the new year, leaving ample time to reflect on the campaign gone by and correct course before the 2027 sprint season kicks off on Feb. 19.

So, for every team whose season has come to a close, what went right in 2026? What went wrong? What must it improve in 2027? Ryan Rosenblatt answers those questions for every eliminated team.

Minnesota United

Supporters' Shield standing: 19th

Cup performance: Round of 16 (U.S. Open Cup), league phase (Leagues Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: It was a miracle that United had a chance to make the playoffs on Decision Day. Despite falling short, their seven-match unbeaten streak to end the season was no fluke as Kelvin Yeboah had four goals and two assists to wrap up an 18-goal season.

What went wrong in 2026: There was a stretch in the middle of the season when the Loons won just one of 18 games and not for any specific reason. They were simply an outright mess for a stretch that made up more than half the campaign.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Usually, teams focus on whom they want to bring in, but the Loons will have to focus on whom they want to keep because they have so many expiring contracts coming up. But they don't have a sporting director after Khaled El-Ahmad left for Austin. Yeboah and Joaquín Pereyra are two good players to keep building around, but how the Loons do so starts with who is in charge; everything else will be on hold until they get that sorted.

LA Galaxy

Supporters' Shield standing: 20th

Cup performance: Quarterfinals (Concacaf Champions Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: The Galaxy attack finished strong, scoring 19 goals in the last seven matches to nearly sneak into the playoffs.

What went wrong in 2026: The season got off to a bad start before it began when Riqui Puig reinjured his knee and was ruled out for the year. It felt as if the Galaxy were scrambling from that moment.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Pick a direction and lay a foundation. There are good players here, but no real direction and it's hard to believe this is the same club that won MLS Cup just two years ago. The Galaxy have been cycling through players and trying to patch things together on the fly for two years, and that can't continue. Whether or not they can rely on Puig going forward, this club needs an ethos for the first time since it won the title and first faced a future without its star.

Colorado Rapids

Supporters' Shield standing: 21st

Cup performance: Semifinals (U.S. Open Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: The Rapids were very good at Dick's Sporting Goods Park, where they went 10-4-3. They also finally spent some money to sign Morgan Whittaker, who delivered five goals after joining them in September.

What went wrong in 2026: There were times when the Rapids looked as good as any team in the league, but even more when they looked as bad as any other. The latter occurred at the end of the season, when the Rapids won just one of their last nine, but it came against the West's best, Vancouver. Consistency was elusive from the start of the season to the finish.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: It's hard to imagine ownership greenlighting anything more than modest spending going forward, but there should be some money left over from the transfer of Lucas Herrington in the summer. If the Rapids can use it to get a quality center back in to pair with Rob Holding, whom they will have to re-sign, then they might have a chance to win their first playoff game in a decade next year.

Red Bull New York

Supporters' Shield standing: 22nd

Cup performance: Round of 16 (U.S. Open Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti both had seasons so good that they forced themselves into the U.S. men's national team, fellow teenager Matthew Dos Santos became a key piece as well, and 21-year-old Ronald Donkor feels like an old head compared to the rest, but he was terrific. The Red Bulls' development system remains as good as any in the country.

What went wrong in 2026: The RBNY attack was simply far too toothless. If they couldn't press their way into good positions and get opportunities in transition, there was no threat at goal.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: This team is desperate for more creativity in the attacking half. The problem is those types of players are usually the hardest to develop and most expensive to sign, and Red Bull GmbH has shown little interest in opening up the purse strings, but they need to spend on a player or two who can threaten defenses with the ball.

New York City FC

Supporters' Shield standing: 23rd

Cup performance: Quarterfinals (U.S. Open Cup), league phase (Leagues Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Nicolás Fernández's first full season in New York was a smash hit. The Argentine scored 16 goals and added 11 assists, sometimes single-handedly carrying the Pigeons' attack.

What went wrong in 2026: Everything from July 31 on. NYCFC were hardly world beaters in the first half of the season, but they were a solid team that was on its way to the postseason. Then they won just two more games and were mathematically eliminated from the playoffs before they even got to Decision Day.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Depth will have to be a focus after injuries ravaged this team and left them desperate to bring in Matt Miazga down the stretch to rescue a flailing defense. The top of the NYCFC team sheet is solid, but it falls apart pretty quickly, and with their new stadium set to open next summer, they're going to want to hit the ground running on the new grass. That means having more than a handful of players they can rely on.

Toronto FC

Supporters' Shield standing: 24th

Cup performance: Preliminary round (Canadian Championship)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: When the Reds got Josh Sargent, Djordje Mihailovic and Niklas Dorsch on the pitch together, they looked like a good team. The club's top signings of each of the previous three transfer windows make up a good spine for TFC to build around.

What went wrong in 2026: Injuries were a problem all season, and that really showed up away from BMO Field, where TFC went 3W-3D-11L.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Sargent showed his quality in his first season north of the border with 10 goals and four assists, but the Reds didn't pay $22 million for that type of production. The defense needs a lot of work, but if TFC want their big-money striker to truly be the star they think he can be, they need to provide a second creative force behind him to pair with Mihailovic.

San Diego FC

Supporters' Shield standing: 25th

Cup performance: League phase (Leagues Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Anders Dreyer put in another great campaign with 14 goals and 14 assists to lead the attack and midseason signing Elias Achouri had some bright moments. The front line was plenty good enough to take San Diego back to the postseason this year.

What went wrong in 2026: It's hard enough to win games in this league with 11 men, but SDFC made a habit of playing with 10. They were shown an astounding eight red cards, undercutting any momentum they may have begun to generate in the middle of summer.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: The defense was putrid and got worse as the season went on, allowing 29 goals in a nine-game winless streak that began at the start of September. The departure of Luca Bombino hurt, but they got $5 million from Stoke City for his transfer, and they need to invest that money in shoring up the back line.

Austin FC

Supporters' Shield standing: 26th

Cup performance: Round of 32 (U.S. Open Cup), quarterfinals (Leagues Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Ervin Torres' debut season went as well as could be expected. The 18-year-old homegrown midfielder was so impressive in the early part of the campaign that he forced his way into the starting XI by late summer, and his passing range could make Austin tick for years to come.

What went wrong in 2026: The team didn't win any of their first nine matches so things started terribly and never got much better. They were bad up front and at the back, and they ended up in a standoff with their own supporters after a fan was ejected for wearing an "abolish ICE" shirt at a game, leading to a boycott. Basically everything went wrong.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Give the new regime the backing it needs to orchestrate a quick turnaround. With Khaled El-Ahmad now installed as chief soccer officer and Jim Curtin taking over in the dugout, that should give Austin reason for optimism. They'll likely get things sorted eventually, but why wait for eventually? Spend some money and get things going in the right direction as soon as possible, and the good news is they don't have to be picky about where to start. The whole roster could use help.

Atlanta United

Supporters' Shield standing: 27th

Cup performance: Quarterfinals (U.S. Open Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Atlanta sent fat checks to European clubs for Emmanuel Latte Lath and Alexey Miranchuk and got little in return, so it was a bit surprising when they went back to the continent for Breel Embolo, but the early returns were good. He scored four goals and added an assist in 11 matches to give the club a well-rounded striker to build around going forward.

What went wrong in 2026: The Five Stripes had their moments in slow, deliberate matches, but were a total mess when the pace of play picked up. That's not going to work in this league.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Atlanta has been a mess since 2019, and in a variety of ways, pivoting leadership and strategy on several occasions, but that might change now. They plucked president of soccer Mauricio Culebro from Tigres UANL in March and now he will decide whether to throw his full support behind chief soccer officer Chris Henderson and manager Tata Martino. Whatever Culebro decides, the Five Stripes need to have alignment and a clear vision starting immediately.

D.C. United

Supporters' Shield standing: 28th

Cup performance: Round of 32 (U.S. Open Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Erkut Sogut was a controversial hire when D.C. tabbed him to be sporting director despite him never working in a club's front office before, but his first signing of last offseason hit as Tai Baribo scored 16 goals after coming over from Philadelphia.

What went wrong in 2026: Unfortunately, the rest of Sogut's moves did not go nearly as well. Louis Munteanu didn't live up to his $7 million price tag, and the hiring of René Weiler flopped as the manager really struggled in his first MLS campaign.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: The big news heading into the winter is United's push to extract hundreds of millions from Washington, D.C. to put a roof over Audi Field and make other upgrades. When that is the biggest source of ambition at a club that has missed the playoffs for seven straight years, you know things are bleak. At this point, fans just want to see the club dream as big on the pitch as they do off of it.

Sporting Kansas City

Supporters' Shield standing: 29th

Cup performance: Round of 32 (U.S. Open Cup)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Sporting were handed a giant reason for hope when Peter Mallouk bought the team prior to the season, and the early signs of his leadership were good. He immediately funneled money into the roster, and the $18 million signing of André Luiz was a smash hit.

What went wrong in 2026: SKC had months to prepare for the offseason under new president of soccer operations David Lee, but few of their winter moves paid off, including the hiring of manager Raphaël Wicky. There was some skepticism around his appointment after an underwhelming stint in Chicago and he did little to overcome those doubts. The squad was always going to need multiple seasons to turn around years of bad squad building, but the talent in the team was not nearly as bad as the results indicated, and that falls on Wicky.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: Expect SKC to continue their rebuild, which should touch every corner of the club, but they made real progress up front in the second half of the season after adding Luiz. The defense, on the other hand, was by far the worst in MLS, and while a new manager can help some of the structural issues, they need to be aggressive in the transfer market with an overhaul of the back line.

CF Montréal

Supporters' Shield standing: 30th

Cup performance: Runner-up (Canadian Championship)

Playoff performance: Did not qualify

What went right in 2026: Prince Owusu proved to be a smart signing when he put up 13 goals in Montréal last season after being plucked from rival Toronto, but he took it to another level in 2026 with 15 goals in his second year at the club.

What went wrong in 2026: Unfortunately, most everything else. They were the worst team in the Eastern Conference, which is difficult to do when you have a top-notch striker, and fired yet another manager. They've now had four different bosses since Wilfried Nancy jumped ship four years ago, and their issues stretched well beyond the pitch too. They alienated their supporters' groups so badly that their biggest fans boycotted the end of the season.

Top offseason priority ahead of 2027: It's hard to decide whether re-signing Owusu, hiring a manager or upgrading about half the roster is most important in Montréal this winter, but the reality is this is a club in distress yet again. Joey Saputo has never been regarded as one of the league's best owners, to be kind, and the club needs investment, especially in facilities with the calendar change coming, as well as stability throughout the organization. It's hard to get the individual things right when the foundation is so shaky. They need a fix at the very top.

stories.headline: Man United shouldn't keep Carrick despite Villa comeback; how Barça beat Atletico
stories.summary: Man United came back to draw Aston Villa, but that shouldn't save Carrick's job. Plus, Barça escape Atletico with victory, and Man City's defensive woes continue.
stories.body:
Before we dive into another international break, Europe's top leagues offered plenty for us to unpack and dissect. Let's begin in the Premier League, where Man United came back from 2-0 and 4-2 down at home vs. Aston Villa to escape with a draw, but we don't think it should end with Michael Carrick being retained as manager.

In LaLiga's big game of the weekend, Atlético Madrid took an early lead over Barcelona only for Hansi Flick's side to battle back and head home with all three points, a result that says more about Diego Simeone & Co. than it does about the defending champions. Plus, we had talking points galore around Manchester City (and their woeful defending), Liverpool (and their work-in-progress win at Crystal Palace), Chelsea (and their woeful defending too), Como (who were knocked back by champs Inter Milan), Real Madrid (who took care of business at Valencia), and much, much more.

It's Monday morning, so what better time for some musings? Let's get into it.

- Man Utd's poor starts have Premier League relegation looking more likely

- Liverpool's Barcola, Isak, Wirtz show signs they're finally starting to click

- Barça pass their biggest test yet as Fermín López sinks Atlético Madrid

Old Trafford mess should change nothing for Carrick ... but it probably will

Meaning that after two rousing comebacks -- from 0-2 to 3-2 in midweek against Roma in the Champions League, and from 2-4 to 4-4 on Sunday against Aston Villa in the Premier League -- he'll probably keep his job. Which is, frankly, absurd. Not because he's necessarily a bad coach, but because there's no reason to have any faith in the plan at the club.

The fact of the matter is that Carrick was appointed as an interim boss and then given a contract because he took them from sixth to third in the table after replacing Ruben Amorim. He was given a two-year deal despite the underlying metrics, Carrick's lackluster CV and lack of top-flight experience, the results being juiced by (unlike this year) the luxury of no European football, and what their eyes told them when they watched the team play.

Nobody expected this season to be quite this bad, but it didn't come out of the blue. And if Zion Suzuki (knocked off balance by Senne Lammens' backside) doesn't miss that desperation cross deep in injury time, United would have lost on Sunday too. And they'd be dead last in the table with seven points, matching their third-worst start ever in England's top flight. But hey, thanks to Lammens' rear -- and Leonardo Balerdi's whiff in midweek, which kept United in the Champions League top 24, rather than hanging with Sabah and Slovan Bratislava near the bottom -- Carrick may well hang on to his job.

Why? Because he's cheap and convenient and the fans aren't blaming him, which means whenever the team shows a spark, they'll get behind him. And that allows the people upstairs who make decisions -- the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada, Jason Wilcox -- to keep hiding. By now, they've obviously built an immunity to the rather milquetoast protests of match-going fans, who clearly have identified the club's issues better than the folks who actually run it.

The Villa game reflected the sort of chaos and drift we've come to expect this season. You can praise the players' self-belief and pride for coming back from two goals down twice (the first time after just four minutes, the second time scoring twice after the 90th minute), but in the same breath you have to question the ineptitude that led to the deficit in the first place.

Carrick (almost certainly, there's enough data out there to be nearly sure) won't take United down, but nor will he take them forward -- certainly not while conditions above him at the club are what they are. The worst-case scenario is that he stays as somewhere between a patsy and a lightning rod. The best-case scenario -- painfully familiar as it may seem -- is another rebuild, except from the top down. No Ratcliffe, no Wilcox and probably no Berrada too (assuming the fallout from the Manchester City case doesn't get him). The Glazers? Well, you're probably stuck with them for the foreseeable future.

A word on Villa, too. Losing in these circumstances hurts -- of course it does -- but they are showing that a big club can operate on a shoestring and get results thanks to a manager who is a legitimate value-add, like Unai Emery. There's a lesson to be learned.

Sunday's big LaLiga game is more about Atletico Madrid losing than ruthless Barcelona winning

Had Barcelona lost on Sunday night, Hansi Flick would have had a bunch of mitigating circumstances. They had no Rodri, the centerpiece of their summer transfer campaign. They were without Jules Kounde and Xavi Espart, which means, once again, a kid with no first-team experience before last month (Brian Fariñas) being chucked into the right back role against Alex Baena. They went down to an early Giuliano Simeone goal, which galvanized the home crowd and allowed Atleti to dictate the game.

Except Atletico didn't. Or, if they did, they did it incorrectly, showing Barça far too much respect and withering, particularly in a wretched second half that saw them manage just two shots, both of them off target. All that footballing capital that we saw in the first 35 or 40 minutes, when it appeared that we might even get a re-run of last year's 4-0 ... gone.

Julian Alvarez, the man on the spot, did great for the assist on Simeone's opener, less so with the two chances he missed, especially the improbable attempted lob of Joan Garcia after the break. I don't have a problem with bringing on Alexander Sorloth at the hour mark, but if you're going to do that, you have to get him involved: instead, he had just nine touches, none of them in the Barcelona box. And while we're at it, though Fermin Lopez showed -- again -- that he's deadly and intelligent and maximizes his talent more than any other Barça player, you can't just lose track of him the way they did for Barça's second goal.

As for Barça, I'm close to giving up trying to second-guess what Flick does with his defensive line. It works for him and he has the medals and wins to prove it -- fine. The back four looked messy and disjointed, at least while Atleti were putting them under pressure (as back lines that include Joao Cancelo often do) and from where I sit, it's not just a question of tactical choices or aptitude, but individual quality. Had Atleti attacked with more gusto and coherence in the second half, it might have been a different story. But they didn't, Barça found immense self-belief from Fermin's goal before halftime and they picked their spots at the right time.

This result was more about Atleti letting Barça back into the game, but it shouldn't take anything away from the visitors' performance. Sometimes, you have to gut it out and take what the opposition gives you. Barça did that brilliantly and now they sit three points clear at the top of LaLiga.

Defensive horror show costs Manchester City at Nottingham Forest

The signs were there. Manchester City hadn't kept a clean sheet in nearly a month. After the 3-1 defeat at Nottingham Forest, in the past eight games they have given up 17 goals. In less than 20 minutes, the visitors were two goals down thanks to more horrendous defending.

Josko Gvardiol shouldn't have lost the ball the way he did, sure, but the rest of the back line reacted in slow motion and seemed to invite Jair Cunha's shot. Liam Delap thundered 40 yards untouched for the second. Forest could have had another when Morgan Gibbs-White overpowered Abdukodir Khusanov. And on the third, Gibbs-White did very well, but again, it was easier than it should have been for Delap.

Enzo Maresca taking off Gvardiol and Marc Guéhi at halftime for Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly may have been about getting more attacking oomph, but it felt like an acknowledgement of defensive failure. The thing is, we know that not only are the four members of City's starting back four excellent players, they're also all central defenders by trade. The question is: Why do they add up to less -- far less -- than the sum of their parts?

There's obviously a mental component to the errors, but there are also aspects to work on tactically, and that's where Maresca needs to earn his bacon. He may also want to reconsider whether a midfield duo of Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernández is viable.

Fernandez with Moisés Caicedo in a two at Chelsea didn't really work consistently in a 4-2-3-1. It's hard to see how it can succeed better at City, especially when the guy ahead of him in attacking midfield is Rayan Cherki (hugely gifted, scored a great goal, but not a big contributor off the ball).

Man City have so much talent that had they taken their chances -- Erling Haaland and Fernández spring to mind -- they may well have won this game, just as they had a considerable xG edge (1.76 to 1.06). The problem is you can't rely on simply outscoring the opposition at this level, because sometimes your shooting boots just aren't on.

Internazionale serve up reality check at Como

It's not that what Cesc Fabregas, Nico Paz and the rest of the guys on the lake are doing isn't fantastic. It's just that maybe it's good to remind ourselves how much experience and top-to-bottom quality matter. And that a side like Inter Milan -- with two Serie A titles, two Italian cups and two UEFA Champions League final appearances in the past four seasons -- is going to have a massive edge in terms of experience and quality, not least because their wage bill, for all Como's spending, is three times higher.

Inter raced to a 2-0 lead inside of 20 minutes thanks to Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram and never looked back, squeezing the life out of Como. All the visitors' fancy play produced just 0.20 xG (to Inter's 1.86), one shot on target (to Inter's four) and 11 touches in the opposition box (to Inter's 34).

Inter manager Cristian Chivu found the right blueprint to stop Como and leveraged his far superior squad to win the game. It helped that he had his best midfield trio fit and able to keep the ball; it helped that both his wingbacks (Federico Dimarco on the left and an outstanding Djed Spence on the right) stretched Como at every opportunity; it helped that even with Lautaro Martínez out, Esposito and Thuram provide more than enough attacking punch. Inter needed to be at their best to have their way with Como and, after some highs and lows this season, they were.

Fabregas took the defeat in stride, noting how these things happen and that Inter punished his team's mistakes. "They could have scored even more against us," he said. "Thing is, playing against teams like them teaches us that we need to be better. It helps ground us. Now we need to learn from it and go on."

Wise words. He'll go far.

Quick hits

10. The sort of Real Madrid that Jose Mourinho wants to see: Valencia away for Mestalla's Last Dance was never going to be much of a soccer test, given how ravaged by debt and bad ownership the once-glorious home side has been. It could have been a test in other ways, however, given the home support's loathing for Real Madrid (even with Vinícius Junior suspended). But Mourinho's crew didn't rise to the bait and by halftime, it was game over. Real Madrid up 2-0 (it would finish 3-0), game controlled (74% possession and 0.05 xG for the opposition) and a sense of inevitability that allowed them to slow the game further after the break.

And another test passed with flying colors in Mourinho's search for balance. Arda Güler coming in from the right offers playmaking and clears the way for Federico Valverde's runs from right back. The Marc Cucurella-Jude Bellingham-Yan Diomande chain dominated the other flank. And Bernardo Silva gives you some tranquillity in the middle. Will this still be the blueprint when Vini is available week in, week out? Can Silva play every game? Time will tell. But, for now, it looks pretty darn good.

9. A stroke of luck and a lot of hard work push Brighton & Hove Albion into second place: The "luck" came in Sunday's 2-0 win over Brentford in the "model club derby." Diego Gómez opened the scoring with a long-range thunderbolt (0.03 xG, which the expected goals gang would turn their nose at) and eight minutes later Igor Thiago got himself sent off for not keeping his cool when Chema Andrés provoked him. Harsh? Maybe, but raise your hands to an opponent's face and you're always at risk and the Brentford center forward obviously forgot this. A goal and a man down, it was game over for Keith Andrews' crew.

Brighton's numbers are pretty staggering. First in goals scored, clean sheets, possession won in opposition third, set piece goals and -- by a huge margin -- in goal difference. Second fewest goals conceded, second in xG and second in "big chances" created. Brighton have been studied (and raided, both in terms of players and staff) by bigger, wealthier clubs yet the secret sauce is still there to the point that you wonder if it's owner Tony Bloom who makes all the difference. In a football world dominated by money and egos, there's something comforting about a side who made a profit in the summer transfer window, with a 33-year-old coach who had never worked in top-flight football sitting in second place on the Premier League table.

8. Paris Saint-Germain win, but so do Paris FC as the City of Lights sits pretty atop Ligue 1: Point taken, it's 11 wins in a row for PSG atop the French league following the 1-0 home win over Troyes. And, sure, maybe they are favorites for a three-peat in the Champions League. But a lot will depend on how much Ligue 1 is taking out of them. PSG have an injury list as long as your arm and seem to be constantly picking up niggling knocks. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is out for the season, Ousmane Dembélé, Marquinhos, Nuno Mendes and Maghnes Akliouche are all out, while Achraf Hakimi was officially "rested" which is an odd thing to do heading into an international break. And the race here is closer than many think.

Liam Rosenior's Paris FC are keeping pace with the big boys. After their win at AJ Auxerre on Saturday, they're just three points back. These two square off on Dec. 12 and it shouldn't be lost on anyone that Paris FC beat Luis Enrique's crew two out of three times last season. Plus, PFC have the luxury of no European football, meaning Rosenior can serve up his high-tempo fare with a week's rest every round. Stranger things have happened...

7. Liverpool can't get carried away, but the win matters after back-to-back losses: Away from home, against an opponent (Crystal Palace) staring down the barrel of relegation and a managerial change and off the back of consecutive defeats, Selhurst Park was always going to be a tough test. Don't let the scoreline fool you. It was; indeed, but for a couple of huge saves from Alisson (who has been rocky this season), Andoni Iraola's crew could have been a couple of goals down. But Alexis Mac Allister popped up when it mattered, we had a Florian Wirtz sighting and coupled with Alisson, it was enough to navigate past Crystal Palace.

This is a work-in-progress and progress is slow, mainly because the pieces don't fit or are injured. Dominik Szoboszlai next to Mac Allister isn't a viable long-term solution. Neither is Ronald Araujo (despite doing well and being a fan favorite) at right back. Neither is Virgil Van Dijk, at 35 with an expiring contract. And doubts persist over Wirtz and Alexander Isak, despite both scoring. It's classic transition season fare. Not great, and not where the manager wants to be, but at least there's forward progress in terms of results. Iraola is showing he can win with grit and making-do, unlike some coaches.

6. It's not always pretty, but Borussia Dortmund find their midfield and keep pace with Bayern Munich: Without the injured Serhou Guirassy, it was Dortmund's midfield that stepped up at home to SV Elversberg. Joey Veerman passed his umpteenth playmaking audition, Jobe Bellingham brought drive, purpose and energy (the apple doesn't fall far from the tree in that family) and Felix Nmecha, who is having his best season yet, popped up with two goals. The visitors came back in the second half, and the late wobbles (and conceded goal) were still there in the 2-1 win, but Dortmund could easily have scored more earlier.

The upshot is that BVB are level with Bayern at the top of the Bundesliga and have lost just once all season long (in the Champions League, away to Bodo/Glimt). It obviously doesn't feel that way to a portion of the fans, who slammed head coach Nico Kovac for what they deemed to be overly defensive substitutions after taking the lead. I'm not a fan of hunkering down while you're head (especially at home) not because of philosophical reasons, but because it backfires too often. But I'm not blaming Kovac here, given Dortmund's historic defensive struggles.

5. Refereeing nonsense, but Arsenal still underperforms despite win: And, you might say, still top of the table, with a lead that has stretched from three to five points. So really, who cares? Fair enough. The win over Hull City wasn't pretty. You're at home against a newly promoted side who haven't won since August, and all you can manage in the first 70 odd minutes is 0.50 xG, mostly from speculative shots. This, while being at full strength (apart from William Saliba -- but Ezri Konsa certainly isn't a problem -- and Bukayo Saka, though Noni Madueke had one of his best games in an Arsenal shirt).

It's not an indictment; it's just further evidence that while Mikel Arteta has tried to make them more expansive this season, we only see it intermittently and last year's DNA continues to loom large. There's also the weird stat of the sudden spike of offside: last year, it happened 61 times. This year, they're on pace for 133. Does it matter? It might at the business end of the Champions League.

A word, too, on the refereeing decision that denied Arsenal a penalty when Nobel Mendy pulled Kai Havertz back while the German was in an offside position. The explanation is unnecessarily convoluted and complicated. Given shirt-pulling is not allowed and it's not as if you're attempting to play the ball, how about just awarding a foul -- and therefore a penalty -- whenever you pull an opponent's shirt in the box, regardless of whether he's onside or not?

4. Bayern still not quite right, and Vincent Kompany can't return soon enough: Stop me if you've heard this one before. Bayern rack up 69% of possession, dominate the game, miss five "big chances" and switch off defensively to scrape a 2-1 win. It feels odd to bring up finishing when you've got a reigning Ballon d'Or who scored 61 goals in all competitions last season, but here we are. Harry Kane did his part recording two assists (though the one for Joshua Kimmich's superb strike was a bit of a "gimme"), but there's no question they're reaping less than they sow, while also getting themselves into needless trouble at the back (witness the Mainz goal or the one that was wiped out by VAR).

Manuel Neuer's injury means we'll see a lot of Jonas Urbig in goal. That may actually bring some stability. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Ismael Saibari and Jamal Musiala are all out, which doesn't help, not in terms of creating chances, but in terms of the sort of tweaks and changes that a good manager makes to maintain control. And in that sense, news that Kompany is set to return after the international break is a godsend. Aaron Danks and Rene Maric are excellent coaches, but they don't come close to matching Kompany's charisma, emotional intelligence and judgement. Not yet, anyway. The thing about great managers is that you often notice them more when they're not there.

3. Roberto De Zerbi won't blame refereeing for Tottenham Hotspur's defeat, but the Jayden Bogle decision made no sense: Kudos to De Zerbi for not looking for excuses to explain Spurs' 1-0 loss away to Leeds United. The answers were there in a subpar second half that saw them outworked and outplayed by Daniel Farke's side, De Zerbi's triple substitution after an hour that somehow made things worse, and poor defending from Archie Gray and Micky van de Ven for Noah Okafor's goal. But losing Mathys Tel in the 43rd minute after the clash with Bogle didn't help either. Not because Tel is some kind of off-brand Kylian Mbappé, but because it forced De Zerbi to rejig his setup by sending on a central striker (Dominic Solanke) for the French winger.

Tottenham have written to ProRef for an explanation of why Bogle wasn't sent off when his boot landed, studs-up, on the back of Tel's ankle. VAR Tony Harrington, in audio released by the Premier League, opted not to call referee John Brooks for a review because it was accidental (Bogle was "stepping into the tackle) and there was a "lack of speed." Therefore, in refspeak, it was "reckless, but not dangerous." This seems insane to me. It obviously was dangerous because Tel was hurt (and came off a few minutes later) and as for the "lack of speed," it's still 150-odd pounds of Bogle coming down on an exposed Achilles' tendon. I'm sure it wasn't malicious, but neither is the officiating consistent here. And if you want to discourage players getting hurt, you can't allow stuff like this.

2. Sunderland defeat exposes all of Chelsea's usual limits: Let's get this out of the way. I don't think Sunderland should have had the penalty that resulted in the only goal of the game. Levi Colwill's contact with Brian Brobbey was minimal and, more importantly, Brobbey had a fistful of shirt. Why referees allow this nonsense is beyond me. That said, Sunderland -- who were bottom of the table and had played Thursday night -- were so much better than Chelsea, they more than deserved the three points.

Chelsea's familiar flaws were laid bare. Cole Palmer is not in a good place right now. Pedro Neto can do many things, but impersonating a center forward isn't one of them. The midfield is an ode to sterile possession and only got worse when, out of desperation, Xabi Alonso moved Moises Caicedo into the back line. Then there's the Brobbey factor. Chelsea made him look like he was Original Ronaldo, Galactus and the Incredible Hulk rolled into one. Sure, he's big and strong and mobile when he gets up a head of steam, but he's still ... Brobbey. The fact is Chelsea looked unprepared for the threat he brings. You expect more from Xabi Alonso and this back line -- the fact that, with Josh Acheampong and Maxence Lacroix missing, his solution to Colwill's difficulties was Caicedo (because Aaron Anselmino was the only defender on the bench) speaks to how poorly constructed this squad is. Even with the massive recruitment operation and the four de facto sporting directors.

1. Distilled cruelty on the final day of the Argentine league: As Carlo Ancelotti says (though pretty sure he wasn't first), "football is the most important of the least important things in life." Those words came to mind watching the final moments of the 2026 Argentine season. Rosario Central, who had welcomed back Ángel Di María for his last dance, were a point behind Boca Juniors, meaning they needed to win and hope in a Boca draw or defeat. They duly beat Estudiantes 2-0 and waited for news from La Bombonera, where it was 0-0 heading into injury time. Players waited and prayed on the pitch, fans did the same in the stands. In that moment, they were one. All they could do was hope. Then came news that Enner Valencia, in the sixth minute of time added on, had scored for Boca. Cue despair ... and then pride. Even as the players wept on the pitch, the fans treated them to a standing ovation. They had given everything and come so close.

That was cruel enough, but it would get worse. Word started making the rounds that Valencia's goal had been disallowed, that the final whistle had gone, that Boca had drawn and Rosario Central were champions. The mournful pride turned to jubilation. Some fans invaded the pitch to celebrate with the players. Except ... Valencia's goal had not been disallowed. Boca had won. None of it was true and as news of reality filtered back into the ground, the celebrations melted away. People were left dumbfounded. The illusion of being champions lasted a few minutes and then it was taken away. My words don't do it justice, watch the video yourself ... if you can bear the sort of wanton cruelty sports can bring.

stories.headline: Who will win MVP? Cy Young? Picks, analysis for 2026 MLB awards week
stories.summary: Baseball's best players and managers of 2026 collect their hardware this week -- starting tonight with the year's top rookies.
stories.body:
The baseball offseason has felt pretty normal so far, at least if you can put the overhanging labor negotiations out of your mind. Some of that normalcy comes from the gradual easing into the initial phases of the hot stove season -- contract options, roster maneuvering, free agency filing -- that point toward next season.

That's administrative stuff, though, and not as fun as the parade in Milwaukee, or this week, when MLB hands out its major awards in what more or less closes the books on the 2026 season.

This year's awards week is an expansion of the usual routine because we have a new honor being handed out by the Baseball Writers' Association of America: the Reliever of the Year Award, which recognizes the top bullpen maestro from each league. Here's how this week's schedule lays out:

Monday: Rookie of the Year (7 p.m. ET, MLB Network)

Tuesday: Manager of the Year (7 p.m. ET, MLB Network)

Wednesday: Cy Young and Reliever of the Year (7 p.m. ET, MLB Network)

Thursday: MVP (7 p.m. ET, MLB Network)

MLB Network will also air the MLB awards given out during a live ceremony in Las Vegas at 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday. Honors given out then include the Hank Aaron Award, Comeback Player of the Year, Mariano Rivera & Trevor Hoffman Relievers of the Year, Edgar Martinez Outstanding Designated Hitter Award and selections for the All-MLB first and second teams.

Finalists for the major awards have already been announced. So let's see how things look before the hardware is handed out. Who might win? Who should win?

Most Valuable Player

American League

Finalists:

Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays

Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals

What to know: Here are the OPS+ figures for the qualifying hitters who ranked second through sixth in the AL: 153, 149, 148, 146 and 144. No. 1? That would be Alvarez ... at 190. He dominated the leaderboards for AL hitters at a Wilt Chamberlain-like level, sweeping all the slash categories and falling one homer and seven RBIs shy of a Triple Crown.

Alvarez made that production count, pacing AL hitters in win probability added (6.9), with a figure that was 68% better than the second-place finisher, Pete Alonso. At 81-81, Alvarez's Astros barely eked out a postseason spot. Without him, they would have been lottery-bound for sure.

Witt should remain a fixture in the finalist group for years to come. He was an easy pick once again this season even though, by his stratospheric standards, it wasn't his best year. He's just so good at so many things that the secondary parts of his game add elite value even when his batting line is more good than great.

AXE did not see Caminero as the third finalist, though it's hard to fault the voters for picking him. From a metrics standpoint, at least the ones that feed AXE, the issue was situational hitting. Caminero ranked fourth in the AL in batting runs above average, but just 12th in the win probability added by all that production.

Doolittle's pick: Alvarez

National League

Finalists:

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

Shohei Ohtani, Los Angeles Dodgers

Brice Turang, Milwaukee Brewers

What to know: AXE and the BBWAA were in lockstep when it came to identifying the finalists. And, really, the drama in this race was more or less over by the time we hit Labor Day. Crow-Armstrong just kept getting better and better while Ohtani struggled with injuries so nagging that he had little impact in October.

The trajectory of the race shows us how much of a tease it was for a few weeks there. After Ohtani built a huge and predictable lead early in the season, Crow-Armstrong took off in June (he posted a 1.249 OPS for the month) and just kept going. By the beginning of August, he had overtaken Ohtani in AXE, and with the Dodgers headed to Wrigley Field on Aug. 3, it felt like we were watching an epic head-to-head race that would be one for the history books.

It was, but only for Crow-Armstrong, who posted one of the best two-way seasons in baseball history. Well, make that three-way. In the subcategories of bWAR, PCA led the NL in both batting runs above average (44) and baserunning runs (9), and ranked third in fielding runs (16). That's how you end up with 9.8 bWAR -- the fourth-best total by a Cubs hitter in the franchise's 151-year history.

Ohtani's greatness is hardly diminished by his 2026 season. Look where he is on this leaderboard despite playing injured for much of the second half of the season. As for the often-overlooked Turang, he'll likely have to content himself with the championship ring he'll get when next season begins. It's a trade-off he'll be happy to make.

Doolittle's pick: Crow-Armstrong

Cy Young

American League

Finalists:

Dylan Cease, Toronto Blue Jays

Parker Messick, Cleveland Guardians

Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees

What to know: Schlittler has been amazingly consistent during his young big league career, and when you're as good as he is, that's a very good thing. Over 51 career starts, including the postseason, Schlittler has a 2.16 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and an average game score of 61.5.

It's hard to believe that, entering the season, we were wondering whether his late-season run as a rookie in 2025 was for real. It was, and Schlittler is one of the best pitchers in the game. His 215 ERA+ was the best by a qualifying Yankees pitcher in franchise history. Better than Ron Guidry, circa 1978. Better than Lefty Gomez, Whitey Ford ... Schlittler tops them all.

When you look at the progression of the AXE leaderboard, it was pretty much a wire-to-wire win for Schlittler, and I suspect he'll be a near-unanimous choice when the AL Cy Young is announced. But it wasn't a runaway. Messick, as a rookie, was almost as good as Schlittler and just as consistent, and Cease came on strong during the second half.

The voters got it right when landing on a top three, and they'll get it right when Schlittler joins Bob Turley, Ford, Sparky Lyle, Guidry, Roger Clemens and Gerrit Cole as the Yankees pitchers who have won a Cy Young.

Doolittle's pick: Schlittler

National League

Finalists:

Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves

Cristopher Sanchez, Philadelphia Phillies

What to know: This could be an interesting vote, though I strongly suspect Misiorowski will win handily. Sanchez has ranked slightly ahead of Misiorowski in AXE all season, largely because of an overwhelming edge in bWAR (8.1 to 6.5) that I don't fully buy into. AXE seeks to balance such measures against each other, but that much of an advantage in one of the two most important categories is hard to overcome. I dug into this race in the final Awards Watch of the regular season.

Ultimately, each of the top six pitchers listed on the AXE leaderboard in this category had an overwhelming season. It was a really good campaign for star-level pitching performances in the Senior Circuit. I favor Misiorowski not just for his dominance -- his league-leading 252 strikeouts and 13 whiffs per nine innings -- but for his consistency. The measure I track related to this is game-score record -- how often a starting pitcher posted a higher game score than the opposing starter on a game-by-game basis. Misiorowski went 25-5 in his 30 starts, easily the best record in the majors.

See that? I made Misiorowski's case and didn't even mention his velocity once.

Doolittle's pick: Misiorowski

Reliever of the Year

American League

Finalists:

Bryan Baker, Tampa Bay Rays

Cade Smith, Cleveland Guardians

Louis Varland, Toronto Blue Jays

What to know: I am a little dubious about the creation of this subcategory of pitching awards, which debuts this season, mostly because the roles of hurlers and the labels that apply to them evolve so much over time, now more than ever. Just to cite one example, here are some numbers for one lights-out reliever this season:

IP: 35 ⅓

W-L: 4-0

ERA: 1.53

K/BB: 36/9

The pitcher in question is Chicago White Sox righty Sean Burke, who compiled these numbers over six relief appearances in the regular season and the playoffs. That average of nearly six innings per relief appearance gives us some crucial context -- these were all bulk relief appearances made in games started by an opener. These numbers weren't compiled by a reliever, per se, but they don't belong in the starter's bucket, either.

All we know for sure these days is that pitchers are pitchers. We have to work hard to measure them in the context in which they are used. More and more, the old starter/reliever distinction is showing wear and tear. I don't think this trend will end any time soon, and I'd hate to see this award become something akin to a regurgitated saves leaderboard, especially because the save is a weak stat to begin with.

Doolittle's pick: I cast a vote for this award, so I'm going to hold off on revealing my pick here. The full voting results will be posted here after the winners are announced. I also blanked out my pick for the Mariano Rivera Award below, because it would naturally be the same pick. I will say that my choices for any award don't necessarily match the AXE leaderboard precisely.

National League

Finalists:

Jhoan Duran, Philadelphia Phillies

Trevor Megill, Milwaukee Brewers

Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

What to know: Miller is the game's most dominant pitcher, and he demonstrated that in every significant measure by which I evaluate relievers. He recorded 129 strikeouts in just 70 innings and did so with pinpoint command, leading all of baseball with a K-BB% of 37.9% -- 6.6 percentage points higher than Misiorowski's, just to draw one comparison. He led all pitchers in win probability added. And he was consistent, earning a 54-12 record in terms of landing above average in WPA on a game-by-game basis, a plus-42 finish that led the majors.

This is a vote that should not be close.

Doolittle's pick: Miller

Rookie of the Year

American League

Finalists:

Kevin McGonigle, Detroit Tigers

Parker Messick, Cleveland Guardians

Payton Tolle, Boston Red Sox

What to know: You can simply glance at a couple of the other AXE leaderboards to get an idea of just how good this AL rookie class was. McGonigle was one of the AL's top overall players as a rookie, and Messick one of the top pitchers. Both have performed at elite levels since entering the majors, and the choice between them is not an easy one.

McGonigle is the favorite and my pick. He was Detroit's best player from the first game of the season, when his grinding approach at the plate was already on full display. He finished 12th in the AL in batting average, sixth in on-base percentage, 14th in OPS and 11th in WPA. At 21, he can get better, too: on defense, against breaking pitches and by adding a little power. The Tigers found a gem.

I extolled Messick's merits above, and you don't need me to tell you that Tolle is a lot more than an epic mustache. But the depth of that AL leaderboard is worth noting. It's really impressive. Carter Jensen isn't likely to earn many votes, but he's already one of the best catchers in the game. Travis Bazzana was a stalwart for a playoff team in Cleveland and is just scratching the surface. And Chase DeLauter will be a fixture for the Guardians for years to come.

Doolittle's pick: McGonigle

National League

Finalists:

Carson Benge, New York Mets

Sal Stewart, Cincinnati Reds

JJ Wetherholt, St. Louis Cardinals

What to know: This is a hard-to-read race, and I'm not really confident in telling you how it will play out. I touted Wetherholt all season, but he struggled over the second half in both performance and durability. Meanwhile, Stewart turned a lot of heads because of his lofty homer and RBI counts, and by the start of September, his metrics were starting to line up with the attention. Then he slugged .280 in September. Benge came on strong at the end, but was it enough?

Ultimately, I'm casting a soft vote for Wetherholt, who finished second to McGonigle in fWAR among rookie hitters. FanGraphs tabbed Wetherholt as the game's fourth-most valuable defender this season (a combination of his fielding performance and positional value) and that carries the day for me. He was also a top-20 baserunner and, despite the second-half swoon at the plate, was still above average for the overall campaign.

Benge is not a bad fallback option, and Stewart did finish third in the majors with 112 RBIs. And hey, I'm not a snob about old-school stats. I love big RBI counts. You just can't rely on them for evaluation, at least not without digging for context. In the case of Stewart, his RBI% (21.4) was strong enough to land him 10th in RBIs above expectation. He was a legit run producer, but didn't do enough in other categories to win my support.

We'll soon see what the voters valued this season.

Doolittle's pick: Wetherholt

Manager of the Year

American League

Finalists:

Kevin Cash, Tampa Bay Rays

Chad Tracy, Boston Red Sox

Will Venable, Chicago White Sox

What to know: Postseason performance doesn't factor into the voting, though my own thoughts on this race did evolve based on my playoff coverage experiences. We'll get into the champion Brewers below, but I didn't spend a lot of time around the Rays this year, seeing them only a couple of times in person before the World Series. When I was able to focus on them more closely, it was clear that a lot of what I liked about Milwaukee's intangibles very much apply to the Rays as well. This is precisely the kind of thing that managers should get credit (or blame) for. Cash has proved for years now that he's one of baseball's very best skippers.

And yet ... Venable's even demeanor, positive attitude and ability to let a healthy clubhouse culture blossom in Chicago amazed me all season. The White Sox thought themselves contenders before they had any right to, and Venable was a big part of that. If these soft factors don't sway you, Venable also gets major props for guiding a taxed and thin pitching staff with a playoff-type paradigm starting weeks before the postseason actually arrived.

Doolittle's pick: Venable

National League

Finalists:

Don Mattingly, Philadelphia Phillies

Pat Murphy, Milwaukee Brewers

Walt Weiss, Atlanta Braves

What to know: I would be surprised if Murphy isn't a unanimous selection to win this award for a third straight season. This is not recency bias based on the Brewers' championship. This was evident weeks before the regular season ended. I just don't know how you can make a case for any other NL manager.

Murphy should become the first manager to win the award three straight years and, obviously, the first to do it in his first three full campaigns. He'd become the 10th manager to win the award at least three times in his career. Pretty impressive for a guy who didn't land his first non-interim big league managing gig until he was 13 days shy of his 65th birthday.

Doolittle's pick: Murphy

Other awards
Just a run-through of my picks for other notable honors, leaving aside the Mariano Rivera Award, since I voted in this category, and the Comeback Player of the Year, which is tough to attack analytically.

Executive of the Year: Chris Antonetti, Cleveland Guardians

There are some great candidates for this award, including Milwaukee's Matt Arnold, who took the honor the last two years when his team didn't win the title. It's also really hard to pick against the miraculous turnaround of the White Sox pulled off by Chris Getz, or the usual most-from-the-least wizardry of Tampa Bay's Erik Neander.

I'm going with Antonetti, who won the award in 2022. My organizational rating metric had Cleveland on top by season's end despite the massive improvement by Chicago, which finished second. The Guardians topped the charts in limiting injury impact and spending efficiency, and finished second, just ahead of the White Sox, in rookie WAR. The race was still close, but Antonetti gets it because of a successful trade deadline that was a big reason the Guardians lasted until the division series.

AL Hank Aaron Award: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

NL Hank Aaron Award: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

Trevor Hoffman Award: Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

Edgar Martinez Award: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

Gold Gloves: The winners have been announced and can be found here. My quibbles:

• AL shortstop: Taylor Walls had a plus-21 DRS (defensive runs saved, per Baseball Info Solutions) but a minus-2 FRV (fielding run value, per Statcast), which is the kind of disparity that makes public-facing defensive metrics so hard to trust. Walls is a defensive wizard who played every day for a World Series team even though he can't hit. That tells you how good his defense is. Nevertheless, Bobby Witt Jr. had the best defensive season at the position and is one of the game's most dynamic and impactful defensive players. He should have won.

• AL second base: The same kind of disparity regarding Walls applies to Cole Young (plus-16 DRS, minus-4 FRV). It's tough, because Young had good prospect grades as a defender, with suggestions that he can hold down the shortstop position. Still, I think Chase Meidroth or Michael Massey would have been better picks.

My All-MLB team:

1B: Pete Alonso, Baltimore Orioles

2B: Brice Turang, Milwaukee Brewers

SS: Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals

3B: Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays

C: Gabriel Moreno, Arizona Diamondbacks

OF: Randy Arozarena, Seattle Mariners

OF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

OF: Fernando Tatis Jr., San Diego Padres

DH: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

LHP: Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves

RHP: Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

RP: Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

stories.headline: Toto Wolff: Mercedes face fierce 2027 battle after winning constructors' title
stories.summary: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.
stories.body:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has played down the suggestion his team is about to embark on another period of dominance in Formula 1, and believes the battle for the 2027 title has already started.

They sealed the constructors' championship with three races of the season remaining at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday, just one week after Kimi Antonelli secured the drivers' championship in Mexico City.

The German manufacturer stole a march on its rivals at the start of the year following the introduction of new engine regulations and has continued to be competitive throughout the season.

But after winning just one race in the last five, Wolff believes rival teams Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari are in a position to pose a serious threat for the title in 2027.

"Look at the last few races, we haven't won," Wolff said. "And today at the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away, it looked like this could be ours, but the competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves.

"It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"So for me, the 2027 season has started now. It is about learning in the three last races.

"What is it we can optimise? What didn't we spot when we put the upgrade on the car? What is it we can learn from today, and attack these last three races full blast, whilst also making sure that we have the learning for next year's power unit and next year's car."

Wolff believes the sheer quality of the top teams on the grid means the era of runaway teams in new regulations cycles -- such as Mercedes from 2014 and Red Bull from 2022 -- is a thing of the past.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row," he said. "And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few titles, but I don't think it's the reality."

- Wet weather mastery by Norris, Verstappen makes Brazil F1's must-see race

- Mercedes completes the double with constructors' title at São Paulo Grand Prix

Wolff believes one of the keys to Mercedes' success remains its no-blame culture and its ability to empower its employees.

"We have stability certainly as a factor, but we have also many people that have joined us recently, and I think what I would like to choose as a word is safety. We are not a high-and-fire organisation.

"We provide a culture and an environment where you can thrive, where you are allowed to make mistakes, where you can speak up. And over the long term, I believe, if you want to be successful, not over a period of a few years, but over many decades, this is what you need to be able to kind of ingrain in the team. And we're trying that.

"It's not something you put on a PowerPoint. You have to live those standards in and out. These are the standards we are setting for ourselves.

"Sometimes we fail, but we look at the long-term vision. For me, soon is in ten years, and I need to set the team up for soon."

stories.headline: AFL Draft: Key dates, FAQs, players to know, and more
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL draft is rapidly approaching, so here's your guide for what to know, including key dates and times, players to know, academy-linked names, and every club's pick.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is fast approaching. Marvel Stadium will once more play host to the first round at 7:00pm AEDT on November 19, with the draft recommencing for the second round onwards on November 20.

Key dates and times
Where: Marvel Stadium

How to watch: Fox Footy

First round: Thursday, November 19, 7pm AEDT

Second round onwards: Friday, November 20, 7pm AEDT

Preseason and rookie draft: Monday, November 23, 3pm AEDT
