State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: What if Manchester United had hired Jurgen Klopp?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are in the relegation zone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Conor McGregor insists it has to be Max Holloway for final UFC fight
stories.summary: Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.
stories.body:
Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.

Back in July, Holloway (28-9) defeated McGregor (22-7) via TKO in just 69 seconds, after McGregor injured his right knee in the opening seconds of their welterweight bout in Las Vegas.

Speaking at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight news conference on Saturday, McGregor, 38, once again reiterated his desire to run it back with Holloway.

"It has to be Holloway," McGregor told reporters.

"Just do the f------ thing again. Just do the thing again. The guy didn't engage once. He's the one that called for the stoppage in the fight. He said 'ref, ref!'

"He's the one stopping the fight. Imagine I just said 'yay!' and jumped the fence. I won! He doesn't want to f------ fight.

"On the one leg, he wasn't coming near me. It's so shocking and so heartbreaking to me and I'm still f------ dealing with it. It has to be Holloway. Just f------ dust it off, re-do it."

On the rehab, McGregor stated he's looking for a return potentially before the summer next year and also hinted if Holloway isn't available he could look elsewhere for an opponent.

"I'm on my way back," McGregor said.

"What's it now November? Three months I'm off of surgery. I done this injury before and returned within nine months. So nine months is pre-summer. I just want to go again and again."

"Something might happen, I don't know. But a fighter that fights me, put some respect on my name. If you're not a world champion fighter, if you've not got world accolades to your name, don't utter my f------ name."

The fight against Holloway at UFC 329 was McGregor's first appearance since July 2021 and he has now suffered serious lower-body injuries in each of past two fights, including a fractured leg against Dustin Poirier in 2021.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Eels recruit to miss NRL opener after ref gesture
stories.summary: Parramatta's marquee offseason recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign -- including the Eels trip to Las Vegas -- after being sinbinned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.
stories.body:
Parramatta's marquee offseason recruit Spencer Leniu is poised to miss the first two games of the 2027 campaign -- including the Eels trip to Las Vegas -- after being sinbinned in Samoa's World Cup semifinal loss to Australia.

Leniu was sinbinned by referee Adam Gee for dissent late in the first half of Sunday's 44-12 loss to the Kangaroos in Sydney.

The prop made a money gesture with his hand as he walked towards the tunnel, a sign that many interpreted as the Samoan forward questioning the integrity and impartiality of match officials.

Leniu was handed a grade three contrary conduct charge on Monday.

The 26-year-old, who will join Parramatta after winning the 2026 premiership with Sydney Roosters, will miss the club's opening two games of the season, which includes their trip to the US to face Gold Coast.

In the unlikely event he contests the charge, Leniu would incur an additional one-game ban if he were to lose his appeal.

The prop's outburst came during a frustrating night for Samoa, from which Samoan halves Ronald Volkman and Jarome Luai have avoided suspension for dangerous contact.

Samoa were on the wrong end of a 9-4 penalty count and coach Ben Gardiner suggested Gee had handed the Kangaroos several "home ground calls".

"It was a real home ground advantage for Australia," Gardiner said.

"They had the the music pumping in the background and we had a lot of Samoan fans here to support us, which was brilliant.

"But they got the home ground calls, got a really good start and then it was just too hard for us to chase back from there."

Brisbane winger Josiah Karapani will also be a late starter next season after he was hit with a two-game suspension by the NRL following a drink driving charge in June.

Karapani, one of Brisbane's best last season, also received an infringement notice for speeding, along with further penalties for failure to display P plates and driving an unregistered and uninsured vehicle.

In court, he was fined $350 and disqualified from driving for three months.

He had already served a club-imposed one-game suspension last season, with the NRL on Monday adding a $1500 suspended fine and obligation to complete an education and training session.

It was his second off-field indiscretion in the season after he was previously stood down by the Broncos for a public nuisance offence in March.

stories.headline: NFL trade deadline grades: Deals for Jessie Bates III, Jacoby Brissett, more
stories.summary: Does Jessie Bates III lift the Jaguars' defense? Wise move for the Ravens to add Jacoby Brissett? Let's evaluate nine trades before the deadline.
stories.body:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline, which is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

Here are our evaluations for nine deals of trading season, including two quarterback moves (Jacoby Brissett and J.J. McCarthy) and the massive blockbuster sending Jeffery Simmons to Chicago. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

Jump to a trade:

Bates | Brissett | Simmons

Buckner | Nelson | Harrison

Jurgens | Porter | McCarthy

Falcons trade S Bates to Jaguars
Jaguars get: S Jessie Bates III

Falcons get: 2027 second-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

Jaguars grade: B

Falcons grade: B+

The Jaguars delivered the opening deal of trade deadline week, acquiring Bates to augment a defense that they hope can be part of a Super Bowl run. Bates is an impact player who delivers splash plays. Over his 3½ years in Atlanta, Bates recorded 14 interceptions and 11 forced fumbles. Yards per coverage snap is a pretty noisy stat for safeties, but over each of his seasons with the Falcons, Bates allowed 0.5 yards per coverage snap or better -- lower than the 0.6 average for the position -- per NFL Next Gen Stats.

He'll take over the spot vacated by Eric Murray, who is out for the season with an elbow injury, and play next to Antonio Johnson. Johnson aligns as a safety only 57% of the time, as he sometimes plays from the box or on occasion even up on the line, while Bates has had more typical alignments. He is 9.5 yards from the line of scrimmage on average, spending 75% of the time at safety and 17% in the box. Despite that he has delivered big plays in the run game, too. He has 13 run stops this season -- plays where the defender makes the tackle on a successful EPA play for the defense -- tied for seventh most among safeties, per NFL Next Gen Stats. He has the best EPA on run stops among safeties (in part because two of his forced fumbles have come on run plays).

I absolutely think it makes sense for the Jaguars to add talent at the deadline as they make a serious push. They currently rank second in ESPN's Football Power Index (and first in the AFC) and have a 24% chance to reach -- and 13% to win -- the Super Bowl. It is fully go time in Jacksonville. The Jags already have a good defense, ranking second in EPA allowed per play, and this will make them better.

Bates is in the final year of his contract with a $13 million salary, and the Jaguars will take over the remaining portion of that money assuming the deal hasn't been altered. I suspect this is a pure rental because the Jaguars currently have just $4 million in 2026 cap space and negative-$15 million in 2027, per OverTheCap.com. But that is perfectly OK.

In fact, if I were the Jaguars, I would rather this be a pure rental. Because the Jaguars are cap-strapped, they won't be active in free agency, which means they are likely to receive a compensatory pick (a fourth-rounder would be my guess) when Bates walks in free agency. If we assume this year's second-rounder is in the back-half of the round and that the Jaguars do get a 2028 fourth-round pick back, this works out to dealing a third-round pick for half a season of Bates, per ESPN's draft pick valuations.

It's a little more than I would want; last week I proposed a Bates deal to Buffalo for a third and a fifth, though I do think now I might have been aiming too low. But ultimately I can get on board because all of the aspects of the deal (impact player, fills need, win-now window) make sense and the price ultimately isn't egregious if he is indeed a rental. So my B grade here indicates I would make this trade if I were the Jaguars, but I wouldn't have done it for more.

Atlanta was somewhat boxed in to making a Bates deal because it has so much cap space -- more than $110 million in 2027, per OverTheCap.com. That means they very likely will be active in free agency and therefore would have a major risk of not getting anything back for Bates if they held him through the end of the year, as acquired free agents cancel out lost free agents in terms of compensatory picks. If the Falcons were not going to be contenders this season, then they almost had to deal Bates for the most they could get for him. And while the 3-5 Falcons are still in the race in the lowly NFC South, they had to ask themselves: Is this team really going to make a run in 2026?

It seems they answered that question honestly. -- Walder

Cardinals trade QB Brissett to Ravens
Ravens get: QB Jacoby Brissett, 2027 fifth-round pick

Cardinals get: 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 seventh-round pick

Ravens grade: B+

Cardinals grade: B

With Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley both hurt, the Ravens are throwing a Hail Mary to save their season. Baltimore is trading for veteran Brissett, shortly after the Cardinals benched him in favor of Gardner Minshew II.

Brissett is a respected bridge quarterback and has played around expectations this season in Arizona. He has a 48.9 QBR, which ranks 23rd out of 30 qualifying starters. That number alone is probably selling Brissett's performance short this season, though, considering he was playing behind the O-line unit that ranked 31st in pass block win rate and was able to use play-action just 18% of the time (27th most). He has posted a plus-5% completion percentage over expectation, per NFL Next Gen Stats (fifth) along with an average 15% off-target rate. And he has been sacked 5.7% of the time (roughly average but notable, given the lack of pass protection). He did throw seven interceptions in eight games, but because he hasn't fumbled yet this season, his turnover rate is roughly average, too.

We can zoom out on Brissett's performance and see a similar picture. Since 2021, he has a 51.1 QBR and a plus-3% completion percentage over expectation (along with a 16% off-target rate), though his QBR was worse than that the past two years. All of this is to say, Brissett is rightfully a fringe starter in the NFL, but that also makes him a substantial upgrade over undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano.

The Ravens lost 33-10 to the Jaguars on Thursday night with Fagnano (and also some Derrick Henry in the Wildcat) at quarterback. In all likelihood, Baltimore's season is over with Jackson currently on injured reserve and the team at 4-5. Ravens coach Jesse Minter has said Jackson's injury is "potentially" season-ending. But Brissett gives the team at least a sliver of hope of staying afloat long enough to hand the reins back to Jackson with a shot at the playoffs.

But make no mistake, those chances are extremely slim. Even knowing Brissett is about to take over at QB (and assuming Jackson has, say, a 30% chance of coming back in games starting in Week 14, ESPN's Football Power Index gives Baltimore only a 3% chance of reaching the playoffs. If Jackson is indeed able to come back, that number goes up, but it's still a long shot. The cost here is low. By ESPN's draft pick valuations, the swap works out to the equivalent of an early sixth-round pick. Considering the team's upside if it does get Jackson back, I think that is easily worth it for Baltimore.

As for Arizona? Brissett's role with the Cardinals always had an expiration date. The team decided to have two bridge quarterbacks on its roster heading into this season and recently turned to the second one in Minshew, while demoting Brissett to third-string. Eventually, the Cards will likely turn from Minshew to Carson Beck, too. So trading Brissett before the deadline was an easy choice; they can recoup some draft value for him and save a few million along the way (Brissett had a $9.7 million base salary this year, and if the contract is untouched, the Ravens will take on the remaining portion of that).

I actually thought Arizona might get a little more for Brissett, because I could have imagined the Vikings -- and maybe the Eagles or Browns -- being interested, as well. But it certainly made sense to deal him, and the Cardinals almost had to make sure they did so before the deadline. -- Walder

Titans trade DT Simmons to Bears
Bears get: DT Jeffery Simmons, 2028 fifth-round pick

Titans get: 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 first-round pick

Bears grade: C

Titans grade: A

This trade is extremely fun. The Bears were already an enjoyable and fascinating team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations. And now they've added one of the game's truly elite defensive players. They also gave up a lot to do so.
The Bears enter Week 8 as ESPN Football Power Index's seventh-best team, with an 80% chance to reach the playoffs and a 13% chance to reach the Super Bowl. When quarterback Caleb Williams has played this season, their offense has produced 0.14 EPA per play, which would be fourth-best in the NFL. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has also been working miracles -- without major turnover luck this time -- but there was a clear need for reinforcements on the defensive depth chart. And now the Bears have landed the best defensive tackle in the league, period.

Simmons has four sacks this season, despite having his pass rush opportunities limited by being on a bad team. He leads all interior linemen in pass rush win rate and ranks fifth in pressure rate. His run stop win rate is above average. And it is hardly a fluke: Simmons ranked second in pass rush win rate (and above average in run stop win rate) while recording 11 sacks last year in a season in which he might have merited Defensive Player of the Year consideration if not for Myles Garrett setting the single-season sacks record.

Simmons is a force and a massive upgrade at an area of weakness. The Bears had been playing 33-year-old Grady Jarrett (who has zero sacks but a solid pass rush win rate) alongside veteran journeymen Kentavius Street, Neville Gallimore and James Lynch. Simmons is an entirely different level of player.

So, Simmons absolutely makes sense for the Bears, and in general, I am strongly in favor of Chicago making deadline additions this season. But there is a compensation limit where a trade ceases to make sense, and I think the Bears ran past it.

Simmons joins a small fraternity of non-quarterbacks to be traded for multiple first-round picks in recent years: edge rushers Micah Parsons and Khalil Mack, offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil, safety Jamal Adams and cornerback Sauce Gardner. The results have been mixed at best for the acquiring team and Simmons, at 29 years old, is the oldest of these players at the time of the deal (Mack was the previous oldest, as the Bears acquired him as a 27-year-old in 2018).

Simmons is under contract through 2030. Assuming that contract is untouched, he will cost $27 million in 2027 and $29.8 million in 2028, with the 2028 base salary becoming fully guaranteed the year prior. That is below what Simmons would make on the open market, but it's still a decent-sized contract for Chicago to take on.

The money saved on Simmons' contract compared to what he would make as a free agent will not reach the expected surplus value of a first-round pick. Even accounting for the high levels of uncertainty in the NFL draft, first-round selections can deliver massive value for NFL teams -- stars on very affordable contracts. The 2027 pick will likely be toward the end of this year's draft, and it seems hard to imagine that 2028 won't be a late first-rounder, too. But I caution against making such strong assumptions -- the Colts didn't think the first-round picks they sent to the Jets last year in exchange for Gardner were going to be as good as they're turning out.

That is the main reason this is a winning trade for the Titans. Tennessee isn't going anywhere this season, and there is little point in keeping Simmons for a few meaningless wins down the stretch while his trade value diminishes. He's a pillar of the organization, but getting that type of draft capital for a 29-year-old player jump-starts the next phase of the team. The question wasn't whether Simmons should be traded, but what they could get in exchange. And they got a great return.

Defenders of the Bears will rightly say surplus value alone isn't everything. The objective isn't to have the highest WAR per dollar; it's to win the Super Bowl. And this move increases the Bears' chance to win the Super Bowl in 2026. Maybe in 2027, too. But it likely hurts their odds from 2028 through 2031.

There are quality defensive players out there who could have improved the Bears' defense while costing them less -- edges Josh Sweat or Yaya Diaby, defensive tackle Daron Payne ... maybe even bringing back Mack. I would have preferred one of those moves. They might have gotten two of those players for less than they gave up for Simmons.

The Bears know they are contenders now, which is why they should go for it. But they gave up too much for a (relatively) older player. Given the player, the need and the situation, it's a move I want to like. But I don't think it can be justified in exchange for two first-round picks. -- Walder

Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers
49ers get: DT DeForest Buckner

Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

49ers grade: A-

Colts grade: B-

As soon as the Colts emerged as a team that might engage in a trade-deadline teardown, it wasn't hard to see the dots connecting Buckner back to the 49ers. That became a reality Tuesday.

Though his numbers have dipped, Buckner, 32, can still help the 49ers get after the quarterback. He has four sacks this season, but his pass rush win rate ranked in the 45th percentile among defensive tackles, alongside a 69th percentile pressure rate. That is a drop from last season, when he was in the 90th and 88th percentile in those metrics, respectively. However, that 2025 performance is a positive sign for what he could bring to the 49ers the rest of this season.

Extra pass-rushing help will be welcome in San Francisco, which ranks 19th in pass rush win rate. The 49ers have been without Nick Bosa, who has been out because of a calf injury since Week 3 but is expected to return soon. Their pass defense is the only one of their major units (run and pass on offense and defense) that ranks outside the top seven in EPA per play (13th).

I'll admit I'm a little surprised the 49ers made this move considering they already have Osa Odighizuwa as a pass-rush-first defensive tackle. But he can play next to Buckner -- especially on passing downs. Also, San Francisco's rash of defensive line injuries makes any help welcome.

This type of roster-bolstering move makes sense for San Francisco. The 49ers are the Super Bowl favorites, according to ESPN's Football Power Index. In fact, they are the favorites by a lot, with the FPI giving them a 23% chance to win the Super Bowl (every other team is below 11%). Adding Buckner to reinforce those chances is worthwhile.

The cost was also quite reasonable. The 49ers are surrendering a fourth-round pick and taking over the prorated remainder of Buckner's $13 million salary, assuming his contract is untouched. While compensatory picks are never a guarantee, there's a decent chance that San Francisco might recoup most of that draft capital back via a comp pick if Buckner signs elsewhere in free agency next offseason, especially given that San Francisco is low on 2027 cap space.

That also is why I'm a little critical of the Colts' move here. Don't get me wrong, it absolutely makes sense for Indianapolis to trade him. The Colts are rebuilding, and Buckner is a 32-year-old in the final year of his contract -- of course they should have dealt him before the deadline.

Perhaps this was the best offer Indianapolis received for Buckner today, but they also didn't have to trade Buckner right now. There are two weeks left until the Nov. 10 trade deadline. I would have thought they could have at least squeezed another Day 3 pick in addition to the fourth-rounder. -- Walder

Colts trade G Nelson to Seahawks
Seahawks get: G Quenton Nelson

Colts get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

Seahawks grade: A-

Colts grade: B+

The reimagination of the Colts is officially underway, with longtime Indianapolis stalwart Nelson heading to the defending Super Bowl champions to bolster the interior of their offensive line.

Nelson, 30, started his career with three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. His level of play dropped in 2022 and 2023, but the 2018 first-round pick battled back to elite form in 2024, when he posted pass block and run block win rates that were each in the 90th percentile, along with earning second-team All-Pro honors. He earned a second-team All-Pro spot last season, too, along with a 91st percentile and 74th percentile pass block and run block win rates, respectively.

His win rates haven't been quite as strong this season (66th and 37th percentile, respectively), but Nelson's reputation is still superb, and having such consistent results the previous two years suggests he probably remains one of the best guards in the league if we're projecting the rest of the season.

The Seahawks presumably will keep Nelson at left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That will push Anthony Bradford, who recently returned from injured reserve and has played two games this season, to the bench. Bradford recorded 30th and 33rd percentile pass block and run block win rates last season, respectively, so Nelson is a substantial upgrade.

The Seahawks have Super Bowl aspirations but must get better play out of an offense that ranks 26th in EPA per play and 31st in EPA per designed rush. They rank 27th in run block win rate, 28th in yards per designed running back carry (3.6) and 28th in yards before contact on designed run plays. They also rank 21st in pass block win rate. So the team needed some offensive line help and upgrading their right guard or center made sense.

Nelson is on an expiring contract, so unless his deal was altered, the Seahawks will take on the prorated remainder of his $16 million in salary for this season, which is a bargain for the quality of play he brings. The Seahawks could sign Nelson to an extension or a new deal after the season, but they could also let him walk in free agency and possibly collect a compensatory pick to mitigate the draft capital lost in this trade.

It makes a lot of sense for the Seahawks to push their chips in on their current team. History tells us how hard it is to sustain elite defensive success, so the Seahawks need to take advantage while they have it.

This was also an easily logical move for the Colts. The 2026 season is lost, and Nelson is a pending free agent. Whatever value he would bring to the team in the second half of the season pales in comparison to what he brings to the Seahawks, and the draft capital return is more than they would get in compensatory picks (which are never a guarantee, anyway) had Nelson left in free agency. Plus, they save money on the remainder of his 2026 salary.

Ultimately, this is a win-win trade. Considering Seattle's contention window, positional (and overall offensive) need, the draft capital required and Nelson's contract, this is a sound move. -- Walder

Cardinals trade WR Harrison to Texans
Texans get: WR Marvin Harrison Jr., 2027 seventh-round pick

Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

Texans grade: C+

Cardinals: A-

Minutes after the Texans completed their 26-3 blowout win over the Titans, news broke that the rumored trade of Harrison, who was inactive Sunday because of the expected move, would be completed. The Cardinals sent him to Houston for a second-rounder and a sixth-rounder in 2027.

Similar to a lot of trades for young players, there are two simple questions: How much of our opinion of Harrison should be shaped by the league's predraft opinion of him and how much should be based on what we've seen from him in the NFL so far?

Harrison was considered a premier wide receiver prospect and was the first non-quarterback off the board with the fourth pick in the 2024 draft. But his production has fallen well short of those expectations to date, with Harrison amassing 1,578 receiving yards over 33 career games.

That equates to 1.5 yards per route run, which is in the 46th percentile among wide receivers who have run at least 15 routes per team game in that span. That number has been even worse in a small sample this season: just 0.6 yards per route run with a much higher percentage of deep fades and go routes (24%) than the previous two seasons (13%). Harrison's player-tracking metrics have been mediocre but not awful during his first two seasons: 47 and 54 overall in ESPN's receiver scores (with slightly better open scores) in 2024 and 2025, respectively.

Despite a rough start, the 1-4 Texans probably still believe they have a Super Bowl-caliber defense and a chance for a postseason run if they can get more talent around quarterback C.J. Stroud, who has been playing well. I don't think that's far-fetched despite their record. This is not the Texans' first attempt to upgrade at wide receiver. After second-year man Jayden Higgins suffered a torn ACL in August, Houston acquired Kayshon Boutte from the Patriots. But Boutte has managed only 1.1 yards per route run despite Nico Collins missing two games.

The Texans will get Harrison for cheap for the rest of this season and next year, and they will have a fifth-year option on him for 2028. But this move is not worth it if Harrison remains the same player he has been with the Cardinals because second-round picks have real value. Receivers who average 1.5 yards per route run can be found quite easily. The Texans are betting that Harrison can reach the upside he showed at Ohio State, including a breakout season in 2022 when Stroud was his quarterback. Having already played two-plus NFL seasons, the chances of a breakout aren't great, but they exist.

I think this trade makes sense for Arizona. The Cardinals didn't have to trade Harrison yet, but he will be worth more to a contending team than he is to them. It's likely his trade value would sink if they waited until the offseason to deal him. And Michael Wilson already had established himself as Arizona's No. 1 receiver.

Ultimately, I would not have made this trade if I were the Texans because the odds of Harrison breaking out immediately feel too low to justify the compensation. But I at least understand the thought process and desire to maximize a loaded roster's chances of making a real run to make the playoffs and win postseason games. -- Walder

Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens
Ravens get: C Cam Jurgens, 2027 seventh-round pick

Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Ravens grade: D+

Eagles grade: A

First, Tyler Linderbaum walked in free agency. Then the Ravens lost Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic to injury, suddenly leaving them without a center. Last week, Baltimore moved first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane to center but evidently doesn't see that as a long-term option.

So Baltimore turned to the trade market and dealt for Jurgens. It's an interesting and unusual move, because Jurgens is no stopgap. He's only 27 years old and is already on a long-term deal after signing an extension with the Eagles in 2025.

Jurgens moved from center to left guard in Week 2 after the Eagles placed guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve. It has not gone well. Jurgens ranks in the bottom three in both pass block and run block win rate at guard. But the Ravens are trading for Jurgens to have him play center.

In 2024, Jurgens was a Pro Bowl center who recorded pass block and run block win rates in the 80th and 50th percentiles, respectively. He made the Pro Bowl again in 2025, but his numbers slipped to the 65th and 39th percentile, respectively. He should be a stabilizing force for the Ravens -- perhaps an average to above-average center -- at what has suddenly become a position of need. But the cost is exorbitant.

The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He's due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens' $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer, per OverTheCap.com. By comparison, Connor McGovern, who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year.

One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens' salary is cheap this season. The Eagles have already paid Jurgens' option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary.

For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson. Jurgens hadn't played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall, who has played center after Jurgens' shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up.

I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday.

So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore's desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. -- Walder

Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys
Cowboys get: CB Joey Porter Jr.

Steelers get: 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Cowboys grade: B

Steelers grade: C+

This is the Cowboys' third trade with the Steelers in the past 18 months (George Pickens and Broderick Jones), and it's their third trade involving a star defensive player after acquiring Quinnen Williams at the trade deadline last season and shipping Micah Parsons to Green Bay last offseason.

It's easy to see what the Cowboys are doing here. DaRon Bland, who first broke onto the scene as a slot corner, was playing on the outside given Dallas' lack of depth. By acquiring Porter, Bland can move back inside, which will allow the Cowboys to relocate 2026 first-round defensive back Caleb Downs, as well. He has been playing the slot, but his natural position is at safety. These are options, not guarantees. Bland might stay outside as the Cowboys instead pursue a strong 1-2 punch at outside corner, with Porter shadowing WR1s.

The salient point is this: Porter can have a rising tide impact on the Cowboys secondary, clarifying the roles of other players and enhancing the whole unit in the process.

Porter is not as tricky of a scheme fit in Dallas as people think, too. His strengths are certainly his length and physicality, such that he can line up in press -- but he has been in press alignments on only 30.6% of his snaps over his career, just above the league average for cornerbacks (24.1%). Porter is a much better man coverage defender than he is in zone, as his passer rating allowed in man coverage over the past four seasons is better than all but Derek Stingley Jr. But the Cowboys are actually running more man coverage (24.8%) under first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker than the league average (23.2%) over the first three weeks.

Of course, early-season rate stats can be noisy. Parker's Vic Fangio-inspired defense will require Porter to play from greater depth than he did in Pittsburgh, and the communication and keys required in that match-heavy system will take some getting used to. But Porter has a valuable and rare skill set in his press-man ability, and premium picks should be spent on players with premium traits. The Cowboys got much, much better in the secondary -- though the move is not without risk.

Acquiring Porter does not solve all their deficiencies; linebacker is still a big problem for this team, and the edge rush isn't far behind. But if the secondary needs less schematic help now that Porter is in play, more coaching tools can be used to hide those other weak spots.

For the Steelers, Porter's recurring back ailments seemed incurable without an extension or a relocation -- what can you do? It's frustrating that GM Omar Khan invested more in third-contract players like Jalen Ramsey and T.J. Watt over a younger, second-contract player like Porter -- Ramsey and Watt will hit their athletic wall far sooner than Porter. Jamel Dean, another third-contract player signed to play corner opposite Porter, now has to cover WR1s alongside Asante Samuel Jr. and 2026 third-round pick Daylen Everette. Corner is no longer a strong position on Pittsburgh's depth chart.

Porter reportedly had contract demands up at the top of the cornerback market, where Devon Witherspoon and Christian Gonzalez recently reset elite deals to clear $33 million annually. I'm not sold that Porter is a top-tier corner deserving of that top money. But because the Steelers let this go on for so long and bleed into the regular season, they were only able to acquire a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for a young, ascendent cover corner. They could have -- and should have -- gotten at least a first-round pick by playing this differently and dealing Porter in the spring or earlier in the summer. -- Solak

Vikings trade QB McCarthy to Giants
Giants get: QB J.J. McCarthy

Vikings get: 2027 fifth-round pick

Giants grade: C

Vikings grade: B+

A mere 22 days after the Giants signed Jameis Winston to a two-year, $13 million extension, New York decided it needed to trade a fifth-round pick for an alternative at quarterback. Of course, a lot has happened in three weeks.

Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2 that is expected to keep him out for at least the regular season. And Winston has delivered two poor performances in Dart's stead, with a 19.0 QBR in relief in Week 2 against the Rams and a 27.9 in Sunday's 12-7 win over the Titans. So in comes McCarthy, the No. 10 pick in the 2024 draft.

McCarthy's pro career has gone poorly so far, which is putting it mildly. He suffered a season-ending knee injury in August 2024, which helped Sam Darnold become Minnesota's starting quarterback. McCarthy was named the starter last season after Darnold departed in free agency but started only 10 games after a series of injuries cost him time. And when he was on the field, the results were not good.

McCarthy posted a 36.1 QBR in 2025 (which ranked 38th out of 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts) and recorded a minus-5% pass rate over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats (43rd out of 45). He threw interceptions at a 4.2% clip (44th), took sacks on 9.4% of dropbacks (40th) and had a 1.8% fumble rate (41st). More alarming is that he did all that while playing for Kevin O'Connell, who has seemingly elevated most of the non-McCarthy quarterbacks he has called plays for.

During training camp, not only did McCarthy lose the Vikings' starting quarterback competition to Kyler Murray, but he then lost the backup competition to Carson Wentz, too. That is a telling red flag.

So why would the Giants trade for him? McCarthy presumably still has some upside based on his draft pedigree, and the Giants are hoping they can profit from him realizing it. But it's hard not to notice the fact that this is John Harbaugh trading for the quarterback his brother, Jim Harbaugh, coached in college at Michigan.

It is difficult to know from the outside which other backup quarterbacks would have been available, but McCarthy still does not seem like an ideal choice. Mac Jones and Spencer Rattler ought to have been the team's first calls (maybe they were). Kirk Cousins probably is off the board with the Raiders sitting at 3-0. Mitchell Trubisky might have been available, considering this already looks like a lost season for Tennessee. And I'm assuming Gardner Minshew II surely must be available, considering he sits in veteran no-man's land between Jacoby Brissett and rookie Carson Beck in Arizona. Stetson Bennett IV could have been an option, too, after the Rams selected Ty Simpson in the first round of this year's draft. I'll grant that some of those options have less upside than McCarthy.

But the Giants' front office should look in the mirror over its bungling of the Winston situation. It's not unreasonable for the Giants to be aggressive in finding a better replacement given how much time is left in the season. But they clearly shouldn't have signed Winston to an extension right before the season if this is how they feel about him!

Even though Murray is a free agent at the end of this season, McCarthy's ship had already sailed in Minnesota after he couldn't beat out Wentz. If he wasn't going to be the Vikings' backup quarterback, his value would likely have continued to drop. To get a fifth-round pick while saving a few million across his remaining 2026 and 2027 compensation (not nothing!) makes sense. They have uncertainty at quarterback in 2027, yes. But that was true whether McCarthy was there or not. -- Walder

stories.headline: Giannis Antetokounmpo 'speechless' over Doc Rivers barbs, warns against 'bitterness or pettiness'
stories.summary: Giannis Antetokounmpo said he was "speechless" over Doc Rivers' recent comments, adding that athletes should not be dismayed by "bitterness or pettiness."
stories.body:
Giannis Antetokounmpo said he was "speechless" over former coach Doc Rivers' comments about the Miami Heat star, adding that he will continue to "focus on my team" and that athletes should not be dismayed by "bitterness or pettiness."

Rivers, who coached Antetokounmpo for parts of three seasons with the Milwaukee Bucks, said during a recent interview that the two-time NBA MVP "didn't want to be the bad guy" and was playing a "game" amid his prolonged exit from Milwaukee.

"Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. And he didn't want to be the bad guy," Rivers told "The Bill Simmons Podcast" in an episode posted Thursday. "He wanted [GM Jon Horst and owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

Antetokounmpo addressed Rivers' criticism Sunday, three days after the interview was published.

"First of all, he's not my coach," Antetokounmpo told reporters after Miami's 114-108 victory over the Sacramento Kings. "My coach is Coach Spo [Erik Spoelstra], but [Rivers] is a guy -- a coach -- that I've worked with in the past. I'm speechless."

After a brief exchange with reporters about the timing of Rivers' comments, Antetokounmpo elaborated.

"You got to go ask him why he thought that," Antetokounmpo said. "That's on him, that's not on me. I just got to focus on my team and what I got to do and how I can be better and how can I help the team.

"But God, that's crazy. Never let bitterness or pettiness get in front of your goals and dreams. For every athlete out there, never let that -- that's insane. But you got to go ask him why he said what he said. Not me."

Rivers, now an analyst for NBC, added that Antetokounmpo "doesn't necessarily have this super IQ" for basketball and that he "really has one way: downhill, force, force."

Spoelstra defended Antetokounmpo when asked about Rivers' remarks, adding that the Heat are making "progress" integrating his style of play into their team philosophy.

"Look, I like Doc and I respect him," Spoelstra told reporters. "This is our business now."

The Bucks' 2025-26 season was largely overshadowed by the question of Antetokounmpo's future with the franchise he led to the 2021 NBA championship. Throughout the season, Antetokounmpo told multiple outlets, including ESPN, that he was committed to the Bucks and would "never" demand a trade.

But sources told ESPN's Shams Charania that Antetokounmpo and his agent, Alex Saratsis, had consistently informed the Bucks since May 2025 that he wanted a trade and believed it was best for both sides to part ways.

Milwaukee ultimately traded Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis to Miami for Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round draft picks, one pick swap and one second-round pick earlier this year.

Antetokounmpo, 31, is averaging 27.5 points and 12.8 rebounds in his first season with the Heat, who have rebounded from a slow start and improved to 4-6 with Sunday's victory in Sacramento.

stories.body:
As usual, it's a small schedule of games on Monday in the NHL. But there's a fun wrinkle this week: three Metro Division teams are traveling to face off against three Pacific Division teams!

No one would say it's a true best-on-best trifecta of matchups given the teams involved, but there are some intriguing facets to each contest.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

New York Rangers at Edmonton Oilers

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | EDM -155, O/U: 6.5

First up on the fight card, the Metro's No. 3 team takes on the No. 1 squad in the Pacific.

These two faced off once already this season -- a 4-1 win for the Oilers in New York on Nov. 1 -- so how does that influence this game?

Connor McDavid had "only" a goal and an assist in that one, well under his 2.61 points-per-game pace this season. Will he put on a show for the home fans?

The Rangers enter this game on a three-game winning streak -- but are 1-5-1 on the road thus far. To improve that record as visitors, they'll need a lot of goals against the high-powered Oilers. The Blueshirts have enviable scoring balance this season; while Alexis Lafreniere is three up on the next closest player in goals (nine), there's a four-way tie behind him.

Philadelphia Flyers at Vancouver Canucks

9:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | PHI -122, O/U: 6.5

In matchup No. 2, the Metro's last-place team takes on the Pacific's. But hey, sometimes these types of games can be fun!

Flyers head coach Rick Tocchet held the same position with the Canucks until the end of the 2024-25 season; he was hired by Philly the next month. Vancouver fans gave him the expected response when he returned last season behind the Flyers' bench; is there any resentment left over when he appears on Monday?

A playoff berth seems outlandish for both teams right now, but there are some fun individual players to check out here. That includes Philly's Trevor Zegras and Matvei Michkov, along with Vancouver's Elias Pettersson and Brock Boeser.

New York Islanders at San Jose Sharks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYI -130, O/U: 6.5

In the nightcap, the No. 5 team in the Metro hits the Bay Area for a showdown against the No. 6 club in the Pacific.

The top draw for each team is their superstar young franchise player -- and both were selected first overall in consecutive NHL drafts.

For San Jose, that's center Macklin Celebrini, the No. 1 pick in 2024. He has 21 points through 17 games, good for a 1.24 points-per-game pace. That's pretty good, but a step down from the 1.40 points per game he scored in finishing with 115 last season.

On the visiting side is defenseman Matthew Schaefer, whose name was called first in 2025. Schaefer is on pace to smash his point total from his rookie campaign (59), with 16 through 16. And, he even had a gloves-on fight against Devils blueliner Luke Hughes on Saturday.

If either of these teams have playoff aspirations, they need to start piling up W's. Monday would be a good day to start!

stories.headline: LA Galaxy miss playoffs again as Real Salt Lake gets final berth
stories.summary: Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.
stories.body:
Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.

Real Salt Lake (13-15-6) snags the ninth and final postseason berth in the Western Conference and will travel to Seattle for a wild-card matchup with the Sounders. The winner will square off against the top-seeded Vancouver Whitecaps in the best-of-three first round.

The Galaxy (11-12-11) have missed the last two postseasons after winning the World Cup in 2024.

Solans and Booth scored three minutes apart to give Real Salt Lake a 2-0 lead in the 13th minute.

Solans used assists from Noel Caliskan and defender Philip Quinton in the 10th minute to score for the 14th time in his first season in the league. Nine of Caliskan's 11 career assists and all three of Quinton's have come this year.

Booth scored unassisted three minutes later for a 2-0 lead. It was the first goal for the 22-year-old rookie midfielder in his 18th appearance and seventh start.

The Galaxy cut it to 2-1 in the 40th minute thanks to an own goal by Real Salt Lake defender Luc de Fougerolles, making his seventh appearance in the league.

Rafael Cabral totaled one save for Real Salt Lake.

JT Marcinkowski saved six shots for Los Angeles.

The Galaxy beat Real Salt Lake 2-1 at home to close out April.

stories.headline: Man United's Patrick Dorgu 'not happy' despite scoring 96th-minute equaliser
stories.summary: Manchester United's Patrick Dorgu has said that he is "not happy" despite scoring a 96th-minute equaliser in the chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday.
stories.body:
Manchester United came from behind twice to seal a point against Aston Villa in a chaotic 4-4 draw on Sunday but it took two goals in injury time, from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu, for Michael Carrick's side to avoid a third defeat on the spin in the Premier League.

Despite nabbing a draw when it looked like they were heading for another loss, United are still in the relegation zone. Michael Carrick's side have eight points after 10 games and sit 18th in the table -- just above Sunderland and Crystal Palace.

United defender Dorgu said that he is "not happy" despite scoring a 96th-minute equaliser against Villa.

"I don't feel happy, we are in a bad situation. We need to fight together to get out of it," Dorgu told Sky Sports after the match.

"A draw is better than a loss but I think we had the better opportunities and we should have won this game."

"Everyone needs to look at himself and ask if he's doing enough. We need to fight for the coach [Carrick] and fight for the club and we need to get out of this together," Dorgu said.

Asked if it "hurts" to be in the bottom three as a United player, Dorgu said: "Of course it hurts but there are a lot of games left."

Matheus Cunha, who scored twice in United's thrilling 3-2 comeback win over Roma in the Champions League last week, also didn't appear particularly happy post-match despite the last-minute draw.

"So tired. I feel so disappointed because, after the other night, we talked a lot about changing our mentality. But we did it again, we conceded some goals. We need to play like Manchester United and go forward and have a bit more courage.

- Sir Jim Ratcliffe chose to appoint rookies at Man United, and it has them facing relegation﻿ fight

- Man United's poor starts have Premier League relegation looking more likely

- Unai Emery storms off, explains exit as Man United equalised against Aston Villa

"And we show character after we concede goals but if you do that before [show character and score goals first] then we can win more games," Cunha said.

When asked why he thinks United are making life so hard for themselves -- by having to come from behind -- Cunha said: "I don't know, to be honest. Everyone is trying to get some answers for that.

"We need to change the mentality to go and do this [score goals] from the beginning."

stories.headline: Pedro Martinez appeals for MLB resolution, reflects on effects of 1994 strike
stories.summary: Pedro Martinez appealed to both MLB players and owners to find a solution to their CBA talks, saying "get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."
stories.body:
Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martinez spoke out about the looming lockout hanging over Major League Baseball, saying a resolution must be found to protect the sport and fans.

"I feel for the fans, and I know when it's good, and it's good, baseball is good right now," Martinez said Saturday, according to the Boston Herald. "So stop the crap around and get something done and don't lock out baseball for the fans."

In Boston for the Pedro Martinez Foundation's 10th annual gala, Martinez said that "honestly speaking, I'm pissed" as he appealed to both players and owners to find a solution.

"Please, for the fans, both sides, figure it out, a good way to get it done, and do not lock out baseball," Martinez said.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. MLB owners are trying to put a salary cap in place. Their latest offer, made Tuesday, would delay the implementation of the cap until 2028.

The players' union has remained steadfast against any talks of a salary cap during negotiations.

Martinez was hurt in multiple ways by a previous baseball stoppage early in his career. At the time of the 1994 strike, he was in his first season with the Montreal Expos, who had the best record in the majors at 74-40 and dreams of a World Series title when play was stopped. The cancellation of the rest of the 1994 season also kept Martinez a day away from arbitration eligibility.

"I hope the commissioner can see me and hear and the players' association hears what I have to say. I might be insignificant, but I lived it before. I experienced that before," Martinez said. "... I was one of the most punished players at that moment because I had talent, and I needed to wait until arbitration to make my money. So I hope they don't mess it up and they don't mistreat the fans."

"Back then, there was a need for other things to change, and they changed for the better. This time, there's no excuse," Martinez added in comparing the 1994 strike to today. "On both sides, not the PA, not the owners, not baseball. The fans do not deserve to be mistreated."

Martinez was a three-time Cy Young Award winner and eight-time All-Star who won the 2004 World Series with the Boston Red Sox and was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2015.

stories.headline: Oscar Piastri splits from Mark Webber's management after eventful seven years
stories.summary: McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has split with the management team headed by ex-Formula 1 driver Mark Webber.
stories.body:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has split with the management team headed by ex-Formula 1 driver Mark Webber.

Webber and his partner Ann Neal had managed Piastri's career since 2019, helping him negotiate his route to F1 by leaving the Alpine junior team and signing with McLaren.

Webber, who started 217 grands prix in his own career, had already reduced his presence trackside this year and a statement indicated a mutual decision had been reached to part ways.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close," Webber said.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career."

Piastri thanked Webber for his involvement in his career to date.

"I'd like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years," he said. "Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career.

"I wish them all the best going forward."

Piastri came within 13 points of becoming world champion last year in a tense battle for the title with teammate Lando Norris and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Now in his fourth season in F1, Piastri made his debut with McLaren after Alpine left a contractual door open for him to leave its junior programme in 2023.

The dispute went to an employment tribunal in late 2022, which ruled in Mclaren's favour allowing Piastri to join the team as Daniel Ricciardo's replacement.

Piastri is currently seventh in the drivers' standings with two podiums this season.

stories.headline: Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer set for spell on sidelines with foot injury
stories.summary: Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.

Neuer had to go off with the injury shortly before halftime in Bayern's 2-1 Bundesliga win at Mainz on Saturday.

Bayern's statement did not give a specific length of layoff for the German goalkeeper, only stating it would be 'for the time being'.

"Manuel Neuer will be out of action for FC Bayern for the time being," the club said.

"The captain sustained a partial tendor tear in his right foot during the German record champions' 2-1 win against 1.FSV Mainz 05 on Saturday, as confirmed by an examination by the FC Bayern medical unit.

"Neuer was substitued shortly before half-time at Mainz."

Replacement goalkeeper Jonas Urbig filled in, as he has often done for the veteran Neuer this season. Urbig is viewed as Neuer's long-term successor at the club and the injury presents a chance to demonstrate he can eventually take the role.

The injury is another blow to Bayern's season following Vincent Kompany's battles with issues that saw him collapse at training. He was hospitalised and treated for meningeal irritation, which is an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord.

Neuer has only made five league appearances this season, while the 23-year-old Urbig has also made five, including his substitute appearance Saturday.

It was a bittersweet moment for Neuer as he also became Bayern's oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days old in the game.
